q1_feeder_simulation_methods.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.
